chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Husayn ibn Abi Saeed al-Mukari, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

A delegation from Yemen came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and among them was a man who was their greatest speaker and the most intense in questioning during his argument with the Prophet (peace be upon him). So the Prophet (peace be upon him) became angry until the vein of anger swelled between his eyes, his face darkened, and he looked down to the ground.

Then Jibraeel (peace be upon him) came to him and said: 'Your Lord conveys His greeting to you and says to you: This is a generous man who feeds food.' So the anger subsided from the Prophet (peace be upon him), and he raised his head and said to him: 'Had Jibraeel not informed me from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that you are generous and feed food, I would have expelled you and made you a topic of discussion for those who come after you.'

The man said to him: 'And indeed, your Lord loves generosity?' He said: 'Yes.' The man said: 'I testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah; and by the One who sent you with the truth, I shall not turn away anyone from my wealth.'
ai.seo_question: How did divine revelation through Jibraeel influence the Prophet's emotional state and interaction with a specific individual?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the interplay between divine knowledge (‘ilm al-ghayb) and human emotion, where Jibraeel’s revelation of the man’s hidden generosity (sakhā’) immediately pacifies the Prophet’s visible anger. It highlights the Shia emphasis on the Prophet’s responsiveness to divine cues and serves as a foundational text for understanding the virtue of charitable giving as a sign of spiritual nobility. The narrative underscores that outward verbosity or argumentativeness does not preclude inner generosity, a key theme in evaluating character in Shia ethics.
